facts.fact: Kiamling 尖叫着把 Hoi 和 Jingling 一并扑倒在地，翻看 Hoi 的头颅与胸口找枪伤，却发现他毫发无伤。
facts.anchor: Kiamling screamed, pulling Hoi and Jingling down to the ground. She looked for the gunshot wounds, eyes roving Hoi’s skull and chest. He was uninjured.

facts.fact: 她跪在林地上，双腿被血浸湿；血是从她身后坡上流下来的，树丛半掩着一头巨虎。
facts.anchor: Her legs were wet where she knelt on the forest floor. Blood. It trickled from behind her, further up the slope. Partially camouflaged by the foliage was a huge tiger.

facts.fact: Archie 面如死灰，手抖得连左轮都掉在地上，他蹲在枪旁干呕；他明白自己打死的不是影子兽，而是一头真兽。
facts.anchor: Archie’s face was ashen. His hand shook so much the revolver fell to the ground, and he squatted beside it, dry-heaving. Not the shadow beast; a real beast.

facts.fact: Hoi 说他看见的是地狱犬，袭击 Jingling 的绝不是橙黑条纹的老虎，但连他自己也说得没把握。
facts.anchor: “I saw it, the hell hound. It was no orange and black tiger that attacked Jingling,” Hoi said, but even he sounded unsure.

facts.fact: Archie 宣称一切都说通了：从来就没有什么影子兽，自始至终只是一头虎。
facts.anchor: “This explains everything! There was never a shadow beast, it was a tiger all along,” Archie said.

facts.fact: Kiamling 几乎是在喊：这解释不了仙女环、魔马、Secretary Peake，还有街道中央冒出来的竹林。
facts.anchor: “Archie, this doesn’t explain the fae ring. The demon horses. Secretary Peake, and a bamboo forest springing up in the middle of a street!” Kiamling was almost yelling.

facts.fact: Archie 脸色一沉——他极想相信这一切都有合理解释——随即承认她说得对，主张去报警。
facts.anchor: Archie’s face fell. He really wanted to believe there was a plausible reason for it all. “You’re right. In that case, we need to inform the police.”

facts.fact: Jingling 的经络全被堵死，qi 仍聚在她丹田如一潭深水，但所有通道都塞住了。
facts.anchor: Jingling’s meridian lines had been entirely blocked. Her qi was still there, a deep pool at her centre, but all the channels were clogged up.

facts.fact: 影子兽与 geongsi、鬼不同：它们饮 qi 是出于嫉妒、想再活一次，影子兽却把 qi 封住，袭击时还抹去记忆，像不愿被看见。
facts.anchor: It was different to how geongsi and ghosts acted. They drank qi, a jealous desire to feel alive again. But the shadow beast stopped it. Erased memories when it attacked, like it did not want to be seen.

facts.fact: Hoi 说警察唯一尽责的对象是那些运回伦敦的金银箱，其余都是借口，无非是杀猪前先把猪打扮一番。
facts.anchor: “The only duty they have is to the chests of gold and silver they’re taking back to London. Everything else is just excuses. Dressing up a pig before you slit its throat.”

facts.fact: Kiamling 挤到两个男人中间把他们推开，说吵下去没用——是中国人不等于就懂北京皇帝的心思，Archie 也不懂维多利亚女王的盘算；她信任 Archie。
facts.anchor: Kiamling wedged between them, pushing them firmly apart. “This isn’t helping. Just because we’re Chinese doesn’t mean we know the mind of the emperor in Peking.

facts.fact: 她坐起身，惊讶地发现 Archie 和 Hoi gor 并没有互相打得鼻青脸肿，而是在打牌，似乎已达成某种休战。
facts.anchor: She sat up, surprised to find that Archie and Hoi gor had not in fact taken lumps out of each other, but were playing a game of cards.

facts.fact: Hoi 递给她一碗八宝养生汤；第一口又苦又冲、几乎让她作呕，随后却浮出久久不散的甜味。
facts.anchor: He handed her a bowl of Eight Treasure revitalising soup. The first mouthful was bitter, sharp, almost making her retch. But following behind it was a hint of sweetness that lingered long on her tongue.

facts.fact: Kiamling 说去报警——这既是给 Archie 的安慰奖，也因为他确实说得对：她需要开始求助；有武器有训练的警察，好过再让妹妹和朋友受伤。
facts.anchor: “We’ll go to the police,” she said. A consolation prize for Archie. But also because he had been right. She needed to start asking for help.

facts.fact: Kiamling 解释广州街头朋友之间以斗嘴代替问候，老阿姨们会为付账互相动手推抢；恭维话只留给客人。
facts.anchor: In the streets of Canton, verbal duels between friends were substitutes for greetings. Old aunties physically fought each other to pay a bill.

facts.fact: Archie 说枪法是 King’s College 的 Thaumaturgy Society 同学教的，他们觉得他不会开枪很稀奇；Kiamling 意识到这是秘密，想套出驱魔之法。
facts.anchor: “Oh, back at King’s College. Some of the other students in the Thaumaturgy Society taught me. They thought it was rather quaint that I didn’t know how.”

facts.fact: Archie 反问 Kiamling 是不是觉得他天真、跟他母亲一样，又说正是这些人给了他教育和职位。
facts.anchor: “You think me naïve, don’t you? The same as my mother. But they gave me my education, my job.

facts.fact: 结尾 Kiamling 怀念自己还抱有更多希望的时光——那时她不必时时设防，可以相信别人的话。
facts.anchor: And yet Kiamling was wistful for a time when she’d had more hope. When her defences were not constantly raised and she could take someone at their word.
